RENEWAL OF A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE RESTRAINING ORDER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

PROTECTED PARTY'S DECLARATION REQUESTING RENEWAL
I, Jordan Lee, declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the following is true and correct. I am the protected party in case number 26FL001234, a domestic violence restraining order issued against Pat Morgan by the Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento County, after notice and a hearing. That order is scheduled to expire on March 15, 2027. I am requesting that the court renew the order under Family Code section 6345. This declaration is informational and does not itself renew, extend, or modify any restraining order -- only a court, after applying the statutory process described in this document, can grant or deny a request to renew a protective order.

SCOPE: RENEWAL OF AN EXISTING ORDER, NOT INITIAL ISSUANCE
This document addresses only the renewal of a domestic violence restraining order that a court has already issued after notice and a hearing under Family Code section 6320 et seq. It does not address the process for obtaining an initial domestic violence restraining order or an order issued ex parte, which this project covers separately in its Domestic Violence Restraining Order (Request for Order) Information Sheet, and it does not address a civil harassment restraining order between people who lack one of the qualifying relationships listed in Family Code section 6211, which this project also covers separately.

ORDER DURATION AND RENEWAL WITHOUT A FURTHER SHOWING OF ABUSE
California's statute caps the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion orders contained in a domestic violence restraining order issued after notice and a hearing at a duration of not more than five years, subject to earlier termination or modification by further court order on written stipulation or on a party's motion. The statute separately provides that these orders may be renewed on a party's request, either for another five or more years or permanently, at the court's discretion, and states expressly that this renewal does not require a showing of further abuse since the issuance of the original order. A request for renewal may be brought at any time within the three months before the orders expire.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion orders contained in a court order issued after notice and a hearing under this article may have a duration of not more than five years, subject to termination or modification by further order of the court either on written stipulation filed with the court or on the motion of a party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6345(a) (California Legislative Information text), five-year cap on order duration, subject to termination or modification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6345.)
  "These orders may be renewed, upon the request of a party, either for five or more years, or permanently, at the discretion of the court, without a showing of further abuse since the issuance of the original order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6345(a) (California Legislative Information text), renewal for five or more years or permanently, without a showing of further abuse (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6345.)
  "The request for renewal may be brought at any time within the three months before the expiration of the orders."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6345(a) (California Legislative Information text), three-month filing window before expiration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6345.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's domestic-violence-restraining-order renewal process -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific order. All three quotations below are drawn from the same subdivision, Family Code section 6345(a), and are treated as one source, not independent sources of each other. This clause does not address what evidence a court considers in deciding whether to exercise its renewal discretion; that is addressed in this document's case-law clauses, which rest on a separate source (published case law interpreting this subdivision).

DEFAULT THREE-YEAR DURATION, AND NOTICE BEFORE EARLY TERMINATION
If the face of the order form does not state an expiration date, California's statute supplies a default: the order lasts three years from the date of issuance. The statute also protects a party who is protected by an order against having it terminated or modified early without notice: if someone other than the protected party files to terminate or modify a protective order before its stated expiration date, the statute requires that the protected party be given notice of that proceeding, and if the protected party cannot be notified before the hearing, the court must either deny the motion without prejudice or continue the hearing until proper notice can be given.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The failure to state the expiration date on the face of the form creates an order with a duration of three years from the date of issuance."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6345(c) (California Legislative Information text), default three-year duration when no expiration date is stated (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6345.)
  "If the party who is protected by the order cannot be notified prior to the hearing for modification or termination of the protective order, the court shall deny the motion to modify or terminate the order without prejudice or continue the hearing until the party who is protected can be properly noticed"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6345(d) (California Legislative Information text), notice-failure consequence when the protected party cannot be notified before a termination/modification hearing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6345.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's domestic-violence-restraining-order renewal and modification process -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific order. The two quotations below are drawn from different subdivisions of the same statute, Family Code section 6345(c) and (d); they are treated as one source (the statute), not independent of each other or of the citations in this document's companion clause on duration and renewal, which cites subdivision (a) of the same section. This clause does not describe the manner-of-service options under Section 1005 of the Code of Civil Procedure or the Safe at Home confidential-address program that the statute cross-references for effecting notice, nor does it address subdivision (e)'s directive to the Judicial Council to create a modification-request form.

THE "REASONABLE APPREHENSION OF FUTURE ABUSE" RENEWAL STANDARD
In Ritchie v. Konrad, a California Court of Appeal addressed, as a case of first impression, the criteria a trial court applies in deciding whether to renew a domestic violence protective order under Family Code section 6345. The court held that a trial court should renew the protective order if, and only if, it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the protected party entertains a "reasonable apprehension" of future abuse. The court clarified that this standard does not require the trial court to find it is more likely than not that future abuse will actually occur if the order is not renewed; it requires only that the evidence show it is more probable than not that there is a sufficient risk of future abuse to make the protected party's apprehension genuine and reasonable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "A trial court should renew the protective order, if, and only if, it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the protected party entertains a “reasonable apprehension” of future abuse."
  — Ritchie v. Konrad, (2004) 115 Cal. App. 4th 1275, 1290 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2281534/ritchie-v-konrad/)
  "this does not mean the court must find it is more likely than not future abuse will occur if the protective order is not renewed. It only means the evidence demonstrates it is more probable than not there is a sufficient risk of future abuse to find the protected party’s apprehension is genuine and reasonable."
  — Ritchie v. Konrad, (2004) 115 Cal. App. 4th 1275, 1290 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2281534/ritchie-v-konrad/)
  Known gap: This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision, used as real evidence of how a California court has interpreted Family Code section 6345's renewal standard -- not a survey of all published or unpublished authority on that standard, and not a claim about how a court in a different state would rule. Both quotations below are drawn from the same opinion and are treated as one source, not independent of each other. This clause does not address the separate evidentiary-factors and collateral-estoppel holdings from the same opinion, which are addressed in this document's companion case-law clause and rest on the same single source.

EVIDENCE UNDERLYING THE ORIGINAL ORDER, AND LIMITS ON RELITIGATING IT
The same Ritchie v. Konrad opinion addressed what a trial court may look to in deciding whether the "reasonable apprehension" renewal standard is satisfied. The court held that the trial judge ordinarily should consider the evidence and findings on which the initial protective order was based in appraising the risk of future abuse if the existing order were to expire. At the same time, the court held that a trial court should not permit the restrained party to challenge the truth of the evidence and findings underlying the initial order, reasoning that allowing such a challenge at the renewal stage would contradict principles of collateral estoppel and undercut the policies supporting those principles.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "the trial judge ordinarily should consider the evidence and findings on which that initial order was based in appraising the risk of future abuse should the existing order expire."
  — Ritchie v. Konrad, (2004) 115 Cal. App. 4th 1275, 1290 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2281534/ritchie-v-konrad/)
  "the trial court should not permit the restrained party to challenge the truth of the evidence and findings underlying the initial order"
  — Ritchie v. Konrad, (2004) 115 Cal. App. 4th 1275, 1290 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2281534/ritchie-v-konrad/)
  Known gap: This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision (the same opinion cited in this document's companion clause on the reasonable-apprehension standard), used as real evidence of how a California court has interpreted Family Code section 6345 -- not a survey of all published or unpublished authority on this question. Both quotations below are drawn from that same opinion and are treated as one source, not independent of each other or of the citations in the companion clause. This clause does not address the opinion's further discussion of whether a trial court may still look behind the order itself when weighing renewal, beyond the collateral-estoppel limit described above, nor does it survey the multi-factor list of considerations the opinion goes on to enumerate.

SIGNATURE BLOCK FOR A RENEWAL REQUEST
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct. Executed on September 10, 2026, at Sacramento, California.

☐ _________________________ Jordan Lee, Protected Party (signature)

This document, including this signature block, does not itself renew, extend, or modify any restraining order -- only a court, after applying the statutory process described in this document, can grant or deny a request to renew a protective order.
